analysis.one_liner: Doubles the IRS's time limit for auditing taxes hidden in offshore secrecy jurisdictions.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one Democratic senator with no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the IRS more time to chase taxes hidden in foreign bank accounts and shell companies in countries that keep financial information secret. Today the IRS generally has three years to audit a return, which is often not enough when records sit behind foreign bank-secrecy laws. The bill would extend that window to six years for anything tied to an offshore secrecy jurisdiction, pause the clock while the IRS waits for foreign records, and extend the collection deadline for people who deliberately hide assets to avoid paying a tax bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who pay what they owe. When wealthy people move income into secret foreign accounts and the IRS runs out of time to audit it, the uncollected tax has to be made up by everyone else through higher rates or deficits. Longer audit windows and faster workarounds for foreign records would help the IRS recover that money.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the IRS audit window from three years to six years for any tax item tied to an account, entity, or transaction in a country whose secrecy rules block U.S. tax enforcement [S3].
Pauses the statute of limitations while the IRS waits on a summons for foreign financial records, so the deadline cannot expire while records are tied up abroad [S3].
Extends the ten-year collection deadline for taxpayers who willfully attempt to evade paying an assessed tax, restarting from the attempt [S3].
Extends the audit window when a taxpayer fails to notify the IRS of certain foreign transactions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy individuals and their advisers who use foreign bank accounts, trusts, and shell companies in secrecy jurisdictions to avoid U.S. tax, plus the offshore financial industry that sells those services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore account holders and secrecy-haven banks

drawbacks.text: The Treasury Secretary would have broad, unreviewed discretion to decide which countries count as 'offshore secrecy jurisdictions,' which could affect legitimate cross-border business and investors who get caught up in the label [S3].
Longer statutes of limitations mean taxpayers, including those with innocent foreign holdings, could face IRS audits of old returns years after filing, increasing uncertainty and defense costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core purpose is straightforward: foreign bank secrecy lets hidden income outlast the IRS's audit clock, so extending the clock where the taxpayer controls the delay targets real evasion. The main costs fall on taxpayers with complex but legitimate foreign affairs, who would face longer exposure to audit and the Treasury's judgment calls about which countries qualify. On balance the bill's costs fall mostly on those using the secrecy system, and its benefits are diffuse but real for everyone else who pays taxes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Ken Salazar introduced the bill on August 2, 2007 [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers using offshore secrecy jurisdictions are better off, since the audit clock against them was never extended. Honest taxpayers, who would have benefited from longer IRS windows to pursue hidden offshore income, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore account holders; no tax enforcement reform

for.name: Sen. Ken Salazar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill for the remainder of the 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 2, 2007 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration of the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; a lone Democrat sponsored it and no senator of either party cosponsored it, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Offshore wealth management (foreign banks, trusts, and shell-company service providers in secrecy jurisdictions)
industries.note: These firms profit from selling secrecy to U.S. taxpayers, and the bill would make that secrecy less useful by giving the IRS up to six years and suspending the clock while records are pursued abroad. Ordinary taxpayers benefit when such evasion is harder to carry out.
Their main protection against IRS pursuit of hidden foreign income is that the three-year audit clock expires before foreign secrecy can be unraveled; the bill removes much of that protection.

industries.industry: International businesses and investors with legitimate foreign dealings
industries.note: The bill carves out publicly traded entities but reaches many ordinary cross-border transactions connected to jurisdictions the Secretary labels secrecy havens, lengthening audit exposure for taxpayers who did nothing wrong.
